rv.q: Betwixt all these sweet affairs of the heart comes some visiting old-actors shtick, a lift from “Hamlet” with a “Godspell” or “Pippin” vibe, similarly reflecting the tastes of the aesthetically glorious early 1970s. David Patrick Kelly and Kevin Del Aguila have no trouble with any of that, charmers ...
The songs – bookending nostalgia anthem Try to Remember, sprightly parenting metaphor Plant a Radish, swooning lovers’ duet They Were You – are as cute and shimmering and simple as ever.

A “Fantasticks” virgin no more, I cannot say I lament missing the original, both because the new version, as noted, doesn’t make major departures from the prior one—it’s a meticulously mounted replica, on a modestly larger scale, of the minimalist, story-theater-style original—and because the whimsy...

The charming new Broadway incarnation of The Fantasticks, lovingly directed and choreographed by Christopher Gattelli, has roots in the show’s storied past; Jason Sherwood’s set begins with a ghost-lit evocation of the original Off Broadway run. But it plants itself firmly in the present, and comes to unexpected bloom.

Every so often, there’s a musical that reminds you just how heavenly a night of theater can be… At a moment when so many Broadway shows are crutched by insipid star casting and overblown vocal gymnastics, Christopher Gattelli’s sublime and heart-tugging revival feels like an antidote to an industry that’s increasingly allergic to simple...

Gattelli’s somewhat spiffed-up production, with Jason Sherwood’s more realistic set than the original, seems fitting for Broadway, but he’s retained most of the show’s simple nature, which is essential for the paper-thin material to land properly.

You’d have to be a hard-hearted cynic yourself to resist the charms of The Fantasticks. This artfully staged revival conjures a nostalgia for plain storytelling, elegant folk melodies with a hint of classicism, and unembellished romanticism — all in a still somewhat intimate setting.

vs.sum: One of Broadway's smallest houses (597 seats) and one of its newest, built in 2015 as Second Stage's permanent home. The intimate scale means excellent sightlines from nearly every seat, though the modern design prioritizes function over grandeur.

acc.note: Elevator from lower lobby to Mezzanine. LOOP system for t-coils and cochlear implants.
